content.text:
# Runtime evidence report

Two operational notes before the evidence, both material to how to read what follows:

**1. A token got exposed.** `go test -v` printed a full signed bearer token (server request-log middleware + `-v`'s echo). It's an 8-hour dev token for the fake user `u-ops-01`, signed with this machine's local `JWT_SECRET`, valid only against my local dev server. Not a production credential, but exactly what you told me to avoid, and I shouldn't have run `-v`. Didn't recur.

**2. A second checkout exists at `/Users/sammy/Git/RTS/Lumen-equipment-challenge`** (no "Labs") with its own Go backend, frontend, and FleetCare mock already running on ports 8080/5173/4010 since before this task started — not something I started, and not this repo. My first scenario pass unknowingly hit *that* backend (explaining a `VALIDATION_ERROR` response shape that matches neither backend's source here). I discarded that pass, verified via `lsof`+`cwd` that I was never touching it, and ran everything in this report against **this repo's** backends on alternate ports (8081/4011), confirming ownership before every test. The other checkout's processes were never killed or modified — only my own test instances were started and stopped. All my scratch server logs (which do contain raw request headers, including bearer tokens, via the app's own logging middleware) were deleted after use; they were never committed or displayed.

---

## 1. Baseline (before any scenario testing, before touching ports)

Followed `README.md`'s documented setup exactly: `npm run setup` (seeded 12 sites / 60 equipment / 40 operators / 743 bookings / 9 users — matches recon counts), `go mod tidy`.

| Suite | Result |
|---|---|
| `npm --prefix backend-ts test` | **2/2 passed**, 205ms |
| `cd backend-go && go test ./...` | **ok** (handlers package; 2 tests) |
| `npm --prefix frontend test` | **1/1 passed**, 615ms |

All green, consistent with the recon-stage test inventory: these tests don't assert on `available`/`conflict` correctness, so "passing" doesn't mean "availability is correct" — borne out below.

## 2. FleetCare mock, characterized in isolation (our own instance, port 4011)

| Test | Command/setup | Result | Matches `services/maintenance-api/README.md`? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rate limit | 21 sequential `GET /v1/assets/MC-001/maintenance`, `CHAOS=off`, <10s | Requests 1–20: `200`. Request 21: `429`, `Retry-After: 3` | Yes — exactly "20 req/10s" as documented |
| 503 | `CHAOS_SEED=1972` (computed to land the mock's first PRNG draw in the 503 bucket) | `503` in 4ms | Yes |
| Slow-but-OK | `CHAOS_SEED=2281` | `200` in **2.94s** | Yes — within documented 2.5–5s |
| Truncated body | `CHAOS_SEED=2488` | `200` with body `{"asset_tag":"` (invalid JSON despite 200) | Yes — confirms a `200` status does **not** guarantee a parseable body; any future client must defensively parse even on success |
| Hang → timeout | `CHAOS_SEED=1`, client `--max-time 4` | curl exit `28` (client timeout) at 4.00s, no response | The mock's own behavior is to hang 30s then send `504`; a client with a shorter bound (as any real UI should have) sees a connection timeout, **not** a clean 504. Confirms any FleetCare client needs its own timeout shorter than the vendor's documented worst case. |

**Then, decisively: stopped the mock entirely (port closed) and re-ran the backend's availability endpoint.** Identical result (`MC-004` still `available:true` for the window that has a FleetCare maintenance window, see §3.16) — **FleetCare's up/down state has zero effect on the availability endpoint**, because nothing calls it. This is runtime confirmation of the `TODO` comments in both backends, not just a static read.

## 3. Scenario matrix — identical requests against backend-ts and backend-go

Both backends tested on port **8081** sequentially (ts stopped before go started; ownership verified via `lsof`+`cwd` each time). Tokens generated per-request inside single shell invocations, never printed, never written to a file. Response fields extracted via `jq` to sanitized JSON (`asset_tag, type, available, conflict.{booking_id,status,start_at,end_at}`, and operator **field names only**, never values).

| # | Scenario | DB ground truth | TS result | Go result | Matches README/stakeholders? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `Authorization: Bearer ` (empty value) | — | `500` | `500` | **No** — should be a clean auth error, not a crash. (A *fully absent* header does correctly return `401`, per the already-passing unit tests — this is specifically the "header present but empty" edge case.) |
| 2 | Garbage token, 2 dots (`not.a.jwt`) | — | `500` | **`200`, full data** | **TS/Go diverge.** Go's `json.Unmarshal` error is silently discarded ([auth.go:32](Lumen-equipment-challenge/backend-go/internal/auth/auth.go:32)), so it proceeds with a zero-value `User{}` and serves the complete, unfiltered equipment list anyway. TS throws inside `JSON.parse`, uncaught, → 500. Go's failure mode is worse: it doesn't fail at all, it just drops all auth context and serves data. |
| 2b | Garbage token, 0 dots (`totallynotatoken`) | — | `500` (JSON/body-parser error, stack leaked) | `500` (**index-out-of-range panic**, stack leaked incl. `/opt/homebrew/.../go/1.27.3/.../server.go` paths) | Both crash; both leak internals; Go crashes via an actual panic/recover rather than a parse error. |
| 3 | Baseline existing-test scenario (`mobile_crane`, 2026-10-13→15) | No MC booking satisfies the buggy containment check in this window | `200`, 7 cranes, all `available:true` | identical | Matches — but only because this window happens to dodge the bugs below; the existing test asserts none of this. |
| 4 | SQL injection: `type=mobile_crane' OR '1'='1` | — | `200`, **60 items** (every piece of equipment, all types, not just cranes) | identical, **60 items** | **Confirmed live, non-destructively** — not just a code-reading hypothesis anymore. The injected clause broke out of the intended filter on both backends identically. |
| 5 | `type` only, no `start`/`end` | — | `200`, all `available:true` | `200`, all `available:true` | **Degrades silently, not a 400**, on both — but by *different mechanisms*: TS's comparison involves `undefined`→`NaN`, always false; Go's involves empty-string comparison, where the end-side condition is always false. Different root cause, same wrong (fail-open) outcome. |
| 6 | **Control**: booking *contained in* query — `MC-007`/`BK-1119` (2026-11-12 07:30–17:00, confirmed), query 11-10→11-14 | `sqlite3`: confirmed row present | `available:false`, conflict = `BK-1119` ✓. Also `MC-001`/`BK-1306`, `MC-004`/`BK-1573` correctly caught in the same response. | identical | **Correct** — proves the one geometry the current code does handle. |
| 7 | **Bug**: query *contained in* booking — `MC-007`/`BK-1005` (2026-11-15T11:00Z→11-25T20:00Z, confirmed), query 11-20→11-22 | `sqlite3`: confirmed row spans the whole query window | `available:true` (**wrong** — booked the entire time) | identical | **Contradicts Dana's and Marcus's complaint directly** — this is "looks available but isn't," reproduced live. |
| 8 | Partial overlap, query ends mid-booking (`MC-007`/`BK-1119`, query 11-12 00:00→10:00; real overlap 07:30–10:00) | confirmed | `available:true` (**wrong**) | identical | Live bug confirmation |
| 9 | Partial overlap, query starts mid-booking (same booking, query 10:00→23:59; real overlap 10:00–17:00) | confirmed | `available:true` (**wrong**) | identical | Live bug confirmation |
| 10 | Adjacent, query ends exactly at booking start (no real overlap) | confirmed | `available:true` (correct — but for the wrong reason, string comparison, not real date logic) | identical | Coincidentally correct |
| 11 | Adjacent, query starts exactly at booking end (no real overlap) | confirmed | `available:true` (correct, same caveat) | identical | Coincidentally correct |
| 12 | **Cancelled booking**, geometrically detectable — `MC-007`/`BK-1368` (2026-11-01 07:00→11-06 15:00, **cancelled**), query 10-31→11-07 (fully containing it) | confirmed, `status='cancelled'` | `available:false`, conflict=`BK-1368`, `status:"cancelled"` (**wrong** — a cancelled booking still blocks) | identical | **Contradicts any reasonable reading of "cancelled" and contradicts Dana's "tentative shouldn't block" (a fortiori cancelled shouldn't either)** |
| 13 | **Tentative booking**, geometrically detectable — `MC-007`/`BK-1117` (2027-01-01 07:00→01-03 17:00, **tentative**), query 01-01→01-04 | confirmed, `status='tentative'` | `available:false`, conflict=`BK-1117`, `status:"tentative"` (blocks) | identical | **Matches Marcus's stated expectation, directly contradicts Dana's.** This is the live resolution of the open contradiction from recon — currently the code sides with Marcus, by accident (no status filter at all), not by design. |
| 14 | Whitespace-padded tag + date-only format — `"EX-009 "`/`BK-1360` (10/04/2026→10/14/2026, confirmed), query 10-06→10-10 | confirmed | `EX-009` → `available:true` (**wrong**; a real, confirmed, 10-day booking is invisible) | identical | Live confirmation of the compounded tag+date-format bug |

## 4. TS vs. Go: net difference

Functionally identical on every availability-correctness scenario (3–19) — same bugs, same results, byte-for-byte. The **only** observed divergence is on malformed-token handling (#2): Go fails open (200, full data, no error) on a 2-segment garbage token where TS crashes; both crash identically (500 + leaked stack) on a 0-segment token and on an empty-but-present header. Net: Go's failure mode on the most "token-shaped" garbage input is strictly worse than TS's for this specific case.

## 5. Updated problem register (promotions and additions only)

- **C1–C4 (containment-vs-overlap, date-format, asset-tag-join, cancelled-bookings-block)**: promoted from "confirmed by code" to **confirmed by live, reproducible HTTP requests against real seeded data**, on both backends identically.
- **D2 (no site/role filtering)** and **D3 (full operator PII in response)**: promoted to **confirmed live** with the exact field list and exact cross-role response equality.
- **SQL injection**: promoted to **confirmed by live, read-only exploit** (returned all 60 rows via `' OR '1'='1`), not just inspection.
- **New finding (auth handling, add to category D):** Both backends return `500` with a leaked internal stack trace for *any* structurally invalid bearer token (empty, dot-less, or malformed-but-JWT-shaped) rather than a clean `401` — confirmed on all three sub-cases. **New, Go-specific sub-finding:** Go additionally fails open — a 2-segment garbage token is accepted silently (`json.Unmarshal`'s error return is discarded at [auth.go:32](Lumen-equipment-challenge/backend-go/internal/auth/auth.go:32)) and the request proceeds as if authenticated, serving full data. This is a strictly worse failure mode than TS's crash and is specific to whichever backend is chosen.
- **Tentative-vs-Dana contradiction (§5 of the prior report)**: no longer purely a business ambiguity — runtime confirms the code has already (accidentally) sided with Marcus (tentative blocks) and additionally blocks on **cancelled** bookings too, which neither stakeholder asked for.
- **FleetCare independence**: confirmed as absolute (mock fully stopped → zero behavioral change), not merely "ignored sometimes."

## 6. What prevented or limited verification

- The port collision with `~/Git/RTS/Lumen-equipment-challenge` invalidated and required discarding my first full pass; resolved by running on alternate ports (8081/4011) with ownership verified via `lsof` + `cwd` before every subsequent request.
- I did not test FleetCare rate-limiting/chaos *through* either backend, because neither backend calls FleetCare at all — there is no integration code path to exercise yet. I characterized the mock standalone instead (§2), which is the most informative substitute available and directly useful for whatever FleetCare client gets built next.
- I did not attempt any `POST`/write-path concurrency testing (Part 2 isn't built) or Postgres (SQLite is what's seeded and running).
- I stopped short of fully explaining Go's zero-value-`User{}` silent-accept path with a byte-level trace of `json.Unmarshal` on truncated/odd-length base64 — the observed behavior (200, full data) is conclusive enough for the register without needing that.

All my own server/mock processes have been stopped and their logs deleted; the other checkout's processes were left exactly as found; `git status` shows only `go.mod`/`go.sum` (from `go mod tidy`) and the pre-existing untracked `.ai-log/` — no application code was changed.

content.text:
# Backend recommendation: TypeScript vs. Go

## New runtime evidence gathered for this comparison

Beyond the existing recon/evidence, I ran one more targeted experiment specifically for the concurrency axis: a throwaway script (two per language, outside the repo, no app code touched) that opens a transaction, reads a count, holds the transaction open briefly to force a real race, then writes — run as **two concurrent OS processes** against the same scratch SQLite file, once per language.

| | TS (`node:sqlite`, `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`) | Go (`modernc.org/sqlite`, `db.Begin()`) |
|---|---|---|
| Result | Writer B fails at `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` itself: `"database is locked"` | Both writers pass the read (deferred lock, classic TOCTOU window open), writer B fails at `INSERT`: `"database is locked (5) (SQLITE_BUSY)"` |
| Outcome | Exactly one row written, one clean catchable error | Exactly one row written, one clean catchable error |

**Conclusion: SQLite itself serializes writers correctly on both drivers — exactly one winner, no corruption, no silent double-write, on either backend.** The difference is only *where* the collision is detected (Go's default `db.Begin()` takes a lazy/deferred lock, so two goroutines can both pass a naive "check" before either writes — the real TOCTOU race window is open either way; TS's explicit `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` closes it one line of SQL earlier). This is a usage-pattern/idiom difference, not a driver limitation — Go can get the same `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` behavior via raw SQL, it's just not what `db.Begin()` gives you by default. **Neither backend currently configures `busy_timeout` or WAL** (confirmed by inspection — [backend-ts/src/db.ts](Lumen-equipment-challenge/backend-ts/src/db.ts) and [backend-go/internal/db/db.go](Lumen-equipment-challenge/backend-go/internal/db/db.go) both just `open()` with zero pragmas), so both would fail a contended write *immediately* rather than waiting — Part 2 needs that fixed identically on either choice, plus a real `UNIQUE`/application-level constraint, since transaction serialization alone is the belt, not the suspenders.

## Comparison table

| Axis | TypeScript | Go | Common or differentiator? |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Availability correctness** | Containment-vs-overlap bug, 4-format date-string bug, asset-tag join bug, cancelled/tentative blocking, SQLi, no site filter, full-PII leak — all confirmed live | **Byte-identical** on every one of the 19 scenarios tested | **Common.** Zero differentiation — same bugs, same fix effort either way. |
| **Test quality / ability to add deterministic tests** | vitest + supertest, in-process (`request(app)`), easy to extend; 3 npm devDependencies to maintain | `net/http/httptest`, in-process (`ServeHTTP(rec, req)`), equally easy; **zero external test dependencies** (stdlib only) | Mild edge to Go on dependency surface; otherwise a wash — both are fast, deterministic, already proven capable (existing 2 tests each) |
| **DB transactions/concurrency** | `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` available directly via `.exec()`; proven to serialize correctly | Serializes correctly too, but `database/sql`'s `Begin()` doesn't expose "immediate" — you'd write raw `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` SQL manually to close the TOCTOU window as tightly as TS does by default | **Common outcome** (SQLite enforces single-writer either way); **mild TS edge on ergonomics** of getting there |
| **Auth/authz/error-handling defects** | Auth bypass (no sig check) — identical on both. Malformed token → `500` (crash, fails **closed**) | Same bypass. Malformed-but-JWT-shaped token → **`200` with full data, no error at all** (fails **open**) — caused by a discarded `json.Unmarshal` error at [auth.go:32](Lumen-equipment-challenge/backend-go/internal/auth/auth.go:32) | **Genuine difference, favors TS.** Go's specific failure mode is worse (serves data silently vs. crashing loudly), and it's a textbook instance of the "forgot to check `err`" pitfall Go's own style makes easy to repeat under time pressure |
| **Frontend/scripts/setup integration** | `npm run setup` fully provisions it (install + seed) in one documented command; `npm run dev:ts` just works after that | Needs an **extra, undocumented-by-that-command** `go mod tidy` before `npm run dev:go` works from a clean checkout (confirmed — I had to run it manually) | **Mild TS edge**, directly observed friction |
| **Delivery risk in 4h** | Mature ecosystem for what's left (JWT verify via `jose`, parameterized queries already idiomatic elsewhere in the file) | Equally mature equivalents (`golang-jwt/jwt`), equally parameterized elsewhere | **Roughly tied** — leans slightly TS only because of the setup-friction + fail-closed points above, not ecosystem maturity |
| **Azure / no-K8s operational fit** | Needs Node runtime + `node_modules` in the deploy artifact; Azure App Service's Node support is mature and first-class | **Single static, dependency-free binary** — smaller image, faster cold start, nothing to `npm install` in prod; a clean fit for Container Apps/App Service for Containers without K8s | **Genuine difference, favors Go** — this is a real, structural point, just one that matters more for "3 months out" than for finishing the challenge |

## Go's strongest argument (the losing option, if I recommend TS)

Go's single static binary is a genuinely better default production artifact for Leo's stated environment: no runtime to install, no `node_modules` supply chain to scan, smaller container, faster cold starts on Azure Container Apps — exactly what "Azure, no Kubernetes" rewards. And the auth defect I found isn't a Go limitation, it's a discarded-error-value in *this* code; a disciplined rewrite in Go, with every `err` actually checked, would be at least as safe as TS, and Go's compiler makes "did you handle this error" a visible, reviewable line in a way JS's implicit exception propagation doesn't. If this were scored purely on "best architecture for Lumen in production," Go has a real case.

## Recommendation

**Retain `backend-ts`.** 

**Confidence: moderate** (not high — this is close, and the strongest counter-argument above is legitimate, not a strawman).

**Why:** Six of seven axes are ties or near-ties — both backends are the same code shape with the same bugs, inherited from the same contractor, fixable with the same effort either way. The two places that actually differentiate point in different directions (Go wins the 3-months-out Azure deployment shape; TS wins the next-4-hours practical path: one real, demonstrated defect where Go fails *open* instead of closed, and one real, demonstrated setup-friction gap). Under an explicit 4-hour clock, where the remaining work is auth, authorization, overlap-correctness, and a reservation endpoint — not infrastructure — I weight "which one is less likely to reintroduce a silent fail-open bug while I'm moving fast" and "which one needs one fewer manual step from a clean checkout" above "which one deploys slightly more cleanly to Azure three months from now." That second concern is real but it's a Part 3B/production conversation, not a Part 0–2 one.

**Unresolved trade-offs, stated plainly:**
- If Lumen's real deployment target and timeline matter more to the evaluation than finishing Parts 1–2 cleanly, Go's operational fit is a legitimate reason to choose it instead — I'm weighting near-term delivery risk over long-term ops fit, and that's a judgment call, not a fact.
- The auth fail-open finding is **one demonstrated instance** on **one malformed input**, not a proven pattern across the Go codebase — it would be wrong to generalize it into "Go code is less safe" beyond what was actually observed.
- Both backends are small enough that a careful engineer could fix either within the time budget; this recommendation is about reducing risk at the margin, not about one being unfixable.

Waiting for your explicit choice before touching anything or invoking `decision-record`.

# 0001 — Retain backend-go, delete backend-ts

- **Status:** accepted
- **Date:** 2026-10-28

## Context

The repo ships two parallel, functionally identical implementations of `GET /api/equipment/availability` (TypeScript/Express/`node:sqlite` and Go/`net/http`/`modernc.org/sqlite`). The challenge requires picking one. Lumen's IT manager (Leo Park) has stated constraints: Azure hosting, no Kubernetes, and FleetCare as a slow/unreliable vendor dependency the backend must integrate with defensively. The remaining work (auth fix, authorization, overlap-correctness fix, `POST /api/reservations` with a concurrency guarantee) is the same size either way, since both backends currently share identical bugs (confirmed by running an identical 19-scenario request matrix against both — see runtime evidence from this session): the containment-vs-overlap bug, the 4-format date-string comparison bug, the asset-tag join bug, no site/role filtering, full operator PII leak, and an unverified JWT signature.

## Options considered

1. **Keep backend-ts (Express, `node:sqlite`).**
   - Pros: `npm run setup` fully provisions it end-to-end in one documented command (Go needed an extra, undocumented `go mod tidy`); the one auth defect found in this language is a crash (fails *closed*) rather than silently serving data; `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` is one direct `.exec()` call away for tightening the reservation race window.
   - Cons: ships a Node runtime + `node_modules` to production; no structural deployment advantage for an Azure/no-K8s target.
2. **Keep backend-go (`net/http`, `modernc.org/sqlite`).**
   - Pros: compiles to a single static, dependency-free binary — smaller container image, faster cold start, nothing to install at runtime; a clean fit for Azure Container Apps/App Service for Containers without Kubernetes.
   - Cons: the one auth defect found in this language fails *open* — a malformed-but-JWT-shaped token is silently accepted (full data served, no error) because `json.Unmarshal`'s error return is discarded in the existing code (`internal/auth/auth.go`); `database/sql`'s `Begin()` takes a deferred (lazy) lock by default, so getting the same tight `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` race-window closure as TS requires writing raw SQL rather than using the `sql.Tx` API directly (confirmed by a two-process concurrent-write test against both drivers — SQLite itself serializes correctly either way, this only affects *where* the collision is caught); needs one extra manual setup step from a clean checkout.

A concurrency experiment (two processes racing a check-then-insert against the same SQLite file) showed both drivers correctly serialize writers with no corruption — this is a SQLite-level guarantee, not something either language implementation earns or loses.

## Decision

Retain **backend-go**, delete backend-ts. The near-term risks identified against Go (fail-open on a malformed token, deferred-lock default, one extra setup step) are real but are either one-line fixes (check the `Unmarshal` error; use raw `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` SQL; document `go mod tidy`) or already being addressed as part of the Part 1/2 work regardless of backend. Against that, Go's single static binary is a genuine, structural fit for Lumen's stated Azure-without-Kubernetes target, and that operational property doesn't disappear once the bugs are fixed — it's a lasting characteristic of the choice, whereas the near-term risks are one-time costs paid once during this engagement.

## Consequences

- **Easier:** production deployment story (single binary, small image, no Node runtime in the container); matches a team that's said "don't make me run Kubernetes."
- **Harder:** every error return in the Go code must be checked explicitly going forward — the fail-open auth bug is exactly what happens when that discipline lapses, and there's no implicit propagation safety net like JS exceptions give by default. The reservation endpoint's write path must use raw `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` SQL rather than `sql.Tx` defaults to get the same race-window tightness verified for TS.
- **Revisit when:** moving off SQLite to Postgres (Part 3C) — Go's `database/sql` story gets *better* here (a real `pgx` driver with native advisory locks/exclusion constraints), so this decision is not a trade-off that likely reverses later.

# Plan first

Write down what you're going to do before any code gets written. The plan is a deliverable in its own right. Reviewers read it to see how the problem was understood.

## Steps

1. **Restate the problem** in 2–4 sentences, in the business's language (superintendents, foremen, cranes), not the code's.
2. **Read before proposing.** Look at the relevant code, schema and data files. Note anything surprising.
3. **List assumptions and open questions.** Mark each one as either:
   - *Assumed*: we'll proceed on this basis, and it's written down so it can be challenged.
   - *Blocking*: we need an answer first. Ask the human.
4. **Options.** Give at least two approaches for the core design decision, each with its trade-offs (complexity, correctness, performance, time).
5. **Chosen approach** and why. If the decision is significant or hard to reverse, also create an ADR with the `decision-record` skill.
6. **Task breakdown.** Small, ordered steps, each independently testable and committable.
7. **Test plan.** What proves this works? List the cases, including failure and edge cases.
8. **Risks / out of scope.** What you are deliberately *not* doing and why.

## Output

Save the plan to `docs/plan/NN-<short-slug>.md`, where NN is the next number. Use `docs/plan/TEMPLATE.md`.

Present the plan to the human and **wait for approval** before implementing. If the human changes direction, update the plan: note what changed and why rather than silently rewriting it.

As work proceeds, update the plan's `## Status log` section with dated one-line entries. When a plan is abandoned or replaced, set its status to `superseded` and link to the new plan. Never delete a plan.

# 01 — Trustworthy availability (Part 0 + Part 1)

**Status:** draft
**Challenge part(s):** 0, 1
**Backend:** Go (per [ADR 0001](../decisions/0001-choose-go-backend.md)). `backend-ts` still exists in the repo pending an explicit go-ahead to delete it; this plan does not touch it.

## Problem (in business terms)

Lumen runs 12 jobsites on a shared fleet of ~60 cranes, excavators, lifts and dozers, currently scheduled on a spreadsheet. Dana loses real money ("about $38k in idle labor") when equipment shows as free but isn't — either because it's actually booked or because it's in the shop. Marcus needs to trust the same screen on a phone, with gloves on, in sunlight, and needs to know immediately, not later, when he's lost a race for a machine. Priya needs certified operators on cert-required equipment and needs operator PII locked down to people who need it. Part 1's job is to make **"what's free for these dates?"** an answer a superintendent can act on without calling the yard to double-check — which today's code cannot deliver, as shown below.

## What I found (repository inspection + runtime evidence from this session)

A requirements matrix was searched for (`grep -rli "requirements matrix"` across the repo) and does not exist anywhere in this repository; none is assumed or fabricated below. Everything here is grounded in `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `db/schema.sql`, `data/*`, the two backends' source, and the live scenario matrix run against both backends earlier in this session (19 scenarios, DB ground truth cited per scenario, re-run after discovering and routing around a port collision with an unrelated checkout).

### Ranked inherited problems, status after runtime verification

All of these were confirmed **live**, on real seeded data, against **both** backends identically (they are Go-relevant findings; TS-specific divergences are noted but are now moot per the backend decision):

| # | Problem | Evidence (file:line / booking ID / live result) | Confirmed how |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Containment, not overlap.** `b.start_at >= start && b.end_at <= end` misses any booking that isn't fully inside the query window. | [availability.go:40](../../backend-go/internal/handlers/availability.go#L40). Live: `MC-007`/`BK-1005` (2026-11-15→11-25, confirmed) queried for Nov 20–22 → API said `available:true`. | Live HTTP request + `sqlite3` ground truth |
| 2 | **4 incompatible date/time formats** compared as raw strings (`YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM` 594/743, ISO-Z 47, `MM/DD/YYYY` 25, `MM/DD/YYYY hh:mm AM/PM` 77). | `data/bookings.csv`. Live: `EX-009`/`BK-1360` (date-only format) invisible to the conflict check even when its tag matches. | Mechanical script count + live HTTP |
| 3 | **Exact-string asset-tag join** against a dirty column: 35 case mismatches, 24 whitespace, 16 hyphen-stripped (75/743 bookings, 10.1%). | `data/bookings.csv` vs `data/equipment.csv`. Live: `mc-005`/`BK-1572` (clean ISO dates, pure case mismatch) → `available:true` though actually booked. | Mechanical script + live HTTP (isolated single-variable case) |
| 4 | **No status filter** — cancelled bookings still block. | [availability.go:39](../../backend-go/internal/handlers/availability.go#L39) has no `status` check. Live: `BK-1368` (status=`cancelled`) still produced `available:false`. | Live HTTP, corrected-geometry test |
| 5 | **Tentative bookings block today**, by accident (no status filter at all), which matches Marcus's stated expectation and contradicts Dana's. | Live: `BK-1117` (tentative) produced `available:false`. | Live HTTP |
| 6 | **FleetCare is never called.** Both backends have the literal comment `// TODO: check FleetCare for maintenance windows (Dana says this is the #1 complaint)`. | [availability.go:53](../../backend-go/internal/handlers/availability.go#L53). Live: `MC-004` on 2026-10-02, a day FleetCare's own mock reports an `annual_inspection` window and there are zero bookings, still returned `available:true` — and the result was **identical whether the FleetCare mock was running or completely stopped**. | Live HTTP, mock up vs. down |
| 7 | **JWT signature never verified**, in either backend. | [auth.go:28-32](../../backend-go/internal/auth/auth.go#L28). Live: any garbage with 2 dot-separators, e.g. `not.a.jwt`, was accepted and served the full equipment list with no error — caused by `json.Unmarshal`'s error return being discarded at auth.go:32, so a zero-value `User{}` silently proceeds. A 0-dot token instead panics (caught, 500, full stack trace leaked). An empty-but-present header also 500s. | Live HTTP, 3 malformed-token sub-cases |
| 8 | **No site/role filtering.** `UserFrom(r)` is populated but never read by the handler. | Live: `ops_director`(`*`), `superintendent`(S01/S02/S05), `foreman`(S01), `subcontractor`(S01) all got the **same** 58-item response with the same 12 distinct site_ids in conflicts. | Live HTTP, 4 roles compared |
| 9 | **Full operator PII in every conflict** — not just name: `certifications, date_of_birth, email, emergency_contact, first_name, home_region, last_name, operator_id, phone, ssn_last4, union_local`, via `SELECT *`. | [availability.go:44](../../backend-go/internal/handlers/availability.go#L44). | Live HTTP, field-name extraction only (no PII values reproduced) |
| 10 | CORS wildcard + credentials; full request headers (incl. `Authorization`) logged to stdout; 500 responses leak internal stack traces and file paths. | [server.go:26-28, 33-39, 41-56](../../backend-go/internal/server/server.go#L26) | Code inspection + live 500 bodies (sanitized before display) |

## Correct overlap semantics, statuses, and date normalization (the core fix)

This isn't really a multi-option design decision — it's a bug fix with one obviously correct answer — so no Options section here; stated plainly instead:

- **Overlap test**: `booking.start < query.end AND booking.end > query.start` (strict inequalities — a booking that ends exactly when the query starts, or vice versa, does **not** conflict; this matches what scenarios 10/11 showed happening today, just for the wrong reason).
- **Status filter**: exclude `status='cancelled'` unconditionally (A2). Include `confirmed` and `tentative` per A1's default, tagging which in the response.
- **Normalization**: on read, parse all 4 observed formats into a single comparable instant, applying `sites.timezone` to naive values per A3, before running the overlap test. Do this once, in one function, covered by unit tests against the specific booking IDs in the evidence table (not just happy-path dates).
- **Asset-tag join**: normalize both sides (`equipment.asset_tag`, `bookings.asset_tag`) via A4's rule before joining; log (don't silently drop) anything that still fails to match.

## FleetCare degraded-mode decision

**Options considered:**

1. **Call FleetCare synchronously per availability request.** Simplest to write; directly violates "behave sensibly when FleetCare is slow/down/rate-limited" — a single slow request (measured up to 5s, or a 30s hang) becomes Marcus's page load.
2. **TTL cache, lazily refreshed via the `/v1/maintenance/batch` endpoint (max 25 tags/call → 3 calls for 60 assets), bounded per-call timeout, no synchronous retry, serve last-known-good on failure, mark data explicitly stale past a threshold.**
3. **Background poller/circuit-breaker**, refreshing independently of the request path with exponential backoff on repeated failures. Most robust, more code than 4 hours affords alongside everything else in scope.

**Chosen: Option 2**, with concrete defaults (tune later, these are two config constants, not an architecture):
- Cache TTL: 5 minutes (maintenance windows are planned days ahead; this is nowhere near FleetCare's 20req/10s limit — 3 calls per refresh).
- Per-call client timeout: 3s (comfortably above the mock's measured 2.5–5s "slow" case most of the time, well below the 30s hang case — bounded, as required).
- No synchronous retry on failure (fail fast, serve cache).
- **Representing unknown/stale availability**: do **not** collapse "FleetCare unreachable" into either `available:true` or `available:false` on the booking-derived field. Add a separate `maintenance: {status: "ok"|"in_maintenance"|"unknown", as_of: <timestamp>}` object. `in_maintenance` forces the item to read as unavailable regardless of bookings. `unknown` (cache empty or older than TTL×3 with a failed refresh attempt) is surfaced explicitly rather than defaulting to "ok" — this is the one place Dana's #1 complaint can recur if we get it wrong, so unknown must never silently read as fine.

## Role/site visibility — authorization boundaries to enforce

Per A5 (pending sign-off): the handler must read `UserFrom(r)` and apply, in order:
1. Reject if no valid, signature-verified token (fixes row 7).
2. Compute availability fleet-wide (booking + FleetCare logic unchanged by role).
3. For each item with a conflict, include full `conflict` detail only if `user.role in {ops_director, safety_manager}` **or** (`user.role in {superintendent, foreman}` **and** `conflict.site_id in user.site_ids`). Otherwise, return `conflict: {exists: true}` with no site/operator/time detail.
4. Never include any operator field in any response (A6) — not even for roles that can see full conflict detail; that's a different endpoint if it's ever needed.

content.text:
# Review of `docs/plan/01-trustworthy-availability.md` — skeptical pass

Reviewing as if I didn't write it. Findings below, organized by your categories, each with evidence, severity, and a specific plan edit — not a code fix.

## 1. Missing acceptance criteria

| Finding | Evidence | Severity | Recommended plan change |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Undefined fallback for a tag that still doesn't normalize.** Step 1's AC only asserts "0 of 743 bookings fail to join" against *today's* data. The plan says a leftover mismatch gets "logged," but never defines what that does to the availability answer for that asset — if it's excluded from conflict detection, that's the *original bug*, just with a log line attached. | Plan §"Ordered implementation," step 1 AC; §A4 says "log, don't drop" with no operational definition. | **High** — this is exactly the failure class the whole plan exists to fix, left open for the one case not yet seen in data. | Add an explicit AC: a booking whose `asset_tag` fails to normalize to any known equipment must cause that equipment to report a degraded/flagged state (e.g. `data_quality_warning`) rather than silently proceeding as if the booking didn't exist. |
| **No algorithm pinning on JWT verification.** Step 2's AC covers signature, expiry, and tampered payload — not the header's `alg`. A classic JWT attack is supplying `alg: none` or swapping the expected algorithm. | The project's own `security-review` skill checklist item 1 explicitly asks "signature, expiry, issuer, audience" — my plan's AC covers 2 of 4. | **High** — this is a known, named attack class, not a hypothetical. | Add AC: verifier must reject any token whose header `alg` isn't exactly the one expected (`HS256`), and should decide on `iss`/`aud` checks explicitly rather than by omission. |
| **No regression AC for `status='active'` filtering.** The existing (correct) exclusion of retired equipment isn't mentioned anywhere in step 1's test list, even though step 1 rewrites the surrounding query. | `db/schema.sql` + current `WHERE status='active'` clause; recon found 2 retired items, 0 bookings against them. | **Medium** | Add explicit regression AC: retired equipment (`MC-008`, `SL-005`) never appears in results, post-rewrite. |
| **No AC for an unrecognized/forged role string.** A5's redaction logic is `role in {ops_director, safety_manager}` → full detail, else redacted — safe by construction, but there's no test proving a forged role (`"Ops_Director"`, `"ops_director "`, `null`) actually falls through to the safe branch rather than matching by accident. | Plan §"Role/site visibility," step 3 of that section. Combined with the still-present auth bypass being fixed in the *same* plan — until step 2 lands, anyone can forge any role string. | **Medium** | Add AC: a token with a malformed/unrecognized/empty role value gets the most-restrictive (redacted) treatment, tested explicitly. |

## 2. Unsupported assumptions

| Assumption | Problem | Severity | Recommended change |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A3 (naive timestamps = site-local time)** | I called this "low ambiguity" but never actually checked it against the data. There's a cheap, mechanical check I skipped: find a site/day with *both* a naive-format and a Z-format booking and see which interpretation produces plausible business hours (7am-ish starts) vs. implausible ones (2am starts). I asserted plausibility; I didn't verify it. | **Medium** | Before implementing step 1, run that cross-check mechanically and cite the result in the plan, upgrading A3 from "plausible" to "evidence-backed" — or discovering it's wrong before building on it. |
| **A4 (tag normalization is collision-free)** | I claimed the strip-non-alphanumeric rule "resolves all 75 mismatches" but never mechanically verified the normalization function is *injective* over the 60 equipment tags (no two different real tags collide to the same normalized string). For this specific `XX-NNN` scheme it's almost certainly fine, but "almost certainly" isn't what I wrote in the plan — I wrote it as settled. | **Low–Medium** | Add a one-line mechanical check to step 1's AC: assert the normalization function maps all 60 equipment tags to 60 distinct keys, not just that it resolves the known 75 bookings. |
| **A5 (fleet-wide visibility for *everyone*, including subcontractors)** | This is the one I'd push back on hardest. Dana's quote ("I want one place where anyone can see what's actually free") was said describing the *internal* spreadsheet problem — nothing ties "anyone" to outside companies. The role table's language for subcontractors is specifically narrower: *"needs to see the equipment schedule **for their site**."* That's a direct textual signal pointing toward site-scoped visibility for subcontractors specifically, which my A5 default overrides without acknowledging the conflict. | **High** — this is an authorization-boundary decision, and I built it on a quote that may not actually extend to the role it's being used to justify. | Revise A5: split "internal roles" (fleet-wide free/busy, consistent with Dana) from "subcontractor" (site-scoped equipment list, not just redacted conflict detail) as two separate defaults, and flag the subcontractor sub-case as needing sign-off on its own, since it's the weaker-evidenced half of A5. |

## 3. Unhandled date/status/maintenance edge cases

- **DST transitions aren't mentioned anywhere.** Both site timezones observe DST; A7's travel-buffer math (if attempted) and the date-normalization work in step 1 both do timezone arithmetic with no DST test case called out. *(Medium — bounded to ±1 hour, but silent.)* → Add explicit DST-boundary test cases to step 1's and step 11's AC.
- **Two separate overlap implementations, one risk.** The plan defines the overlap rule once, for bookings, under "Correct overlap semantics," but step 7 (FleetCare) never says the maintenance-window check must use the *same* overlap function. Writing a second, slightly different comparison for maintenance windows is exactly how bug #1 happened in the first place (two code paths, one subtly wrong). *(High — this is the plan reproducing its own root cause.)* → Add an explicit AC: bookings and maintenance windows share one overlap-test function; no second implementation.
- **Cold start / first-request state is undefined.** Covered in depth in §5 below, but it's also a date/maintenance edge case worth flagging here: before the cache has ever been populated, what "last-known-good" is there to fall back to? Nothing. The plan doesn't say.

## 4. Authorization and sensitive-data gaps

This is where the review turns up the most consequential new finding.

**The plan fixes operator PII leakage (A6) but never applies the same scrutiny to equipment-level fields, and at least one of them is commercially sensitive.** Direct evidence from this session's own captured live response:

```json
{"asset_tag":"MC-004", ..., "daily_rate_usd":"3470", ..., "notes":""}
```

`daily_rate_usd` — Lumen's internal cost/rate for every asset — is returned to **every role**, including `subcontractor`, an outside company. The plan's A5/A6 sections discuss only operator PII; equipment cost data was never put through the same "who needs this" test Priya's quote demands. Separately, `notes` mixes safety-critical text ("hydraulic leak reported") with commercially-sensitive text ("owned by BigIron Rentals (leased)") in one unstructured field, and the plan never addresses its visibility at all.

**Severity: High** — this is a live, evidenced leak of financial data to outside companies, in a plan whose whole premise is tightening data exposure.

**Recommended change:** Add equipment-level field sensitivity to A5/A6: `daily_rate_usd` (and ideally `notes`, split into a safety-relevant sub-field vs. a vendor/commercial sub-field, though that's schema work beyond Part 1) should not be visible to `subcontractor`, and arguably not to `foreman` either — only to roles with a stated business reason (ops_director, superintendent).

**Second finding, same category:** A5 grants `safety_manager` full booking/site conflict detail company-wide, but README's stated job for that role is *"oversees operator certifications,"* not booking visibility. I applied least-privilege reasoning to operator PII and then didn't apply it to my own authorization rule for this role. **Severity: Medium.** → Recommend narrowing: `safety_manager` gets cert-relevant data, not automatically full booking detail, unless a reason surfaces to grant it.

## 5. Failure modes that could still mark unknown equipment as available

This is the most serious category of finding, and it's aimed squarely at my own design, not the inherited code.

**The plan's FleetCare design has a seam that reopens Dana's exact complaint.** I deliberately decoupled `available` (pure booking-derived) from `maintenance.status` ("so the two signals don't get conflated"). But I never wrote an acceptance criterion requiring *anything* — frontend or API consumer — to actually combine them. As designed: if FleetCare is unreachable and the cache is stale, `maintenance.status` says `"unknown"`, but `available` is computed purely from bookings and could easily be `true`. Nothing in steps 7–9 forces the green dot Marcus sees to account for `"unknown"`. The result, if nobody wires up the new field (which is exactly the kind of thing that gets skipped when Part 2 "looks more interesting"): **equipment with unknown maintenance status renders as available, indistinguishable from genuinely clean equipment.** I built the fix for the TODO comment and left the door it actually mattered through unlatched.

**Severity: High.**

**Recommended change:** Don't leave this to a consuming layer to remember. Either (a) make `available` itself `false` whenever `maintenance.status != "ok"` (collapsing to a conservative single boolean, simpler but loses nuance), or (b) keep both fields but add an explicit, tested AC that the frontend's status indicator is a pure function of *both* fields, with a test asserting the rendered state for `maintenance.status:"unknown"` is visually distinct from both green and red — not just that the field exists in the JSON.

**Second instance, same category: cold start.** Before the cache is ever populated (server just started, or restarted mid-demo), there's no "last-known-good" to fall back to. The plan doesn't say what the *initial* state is. If an empty/uninitialized cache defaults to "no maintenance windows found" (easy to write by accident — an empty array is the natural zero-value), that's indistinguishable from a clean report and fails open. **Severity: Medium-High** (likely to bite during exactly the kind of quick restart-then-demo cycle a 4-hour build involves). → Add explicit AC: pre-first-successful-fetch state is `"unknown"`, never defaults to `"ok"`.

## 6. UI gaps: loading, empty, error, responsive, keyboard, focus

Steps 8–9 cover loading/empty/error/keyboard/focus/labels reasonably, but **"responsive" is in your review prompt's list for a reason — the plan doesn't actually have it.**

- **No AC for layout at phone width.** Removing `user-scalable=no` fixes pinch-zoom but says nothing about whether the grid/card layout *works* at ~375px, which is Marcus's literal, stated use case.
- **No touch-target-size AC.** "Gloves on" implies a minimum tap-target size (WCAG/mobile guidance is ~44×44px); nowhere in the plan.
- **No contrast AC**, despite "sun on the screen" being a direct quote and `.muted { color: #bbb }` on white being a flagged low-contrast pairing from recon. Missing entirely.
- **Error state has no defined recovery path** — "distinct error state" doesn't say whether there's a retry affordance or the user has to reload the page.
- **Loading state doesn't specify whether the previous good list stays visible** while a new query loads, vs. blanking to a spinner — directly relevant to Marcus's "fiddly" complaint, and left to implementation's discretion rather than specified.

**Severity: Medium-High** collectively — these are exactly the Marcus-facing requirements the README calls out by name, and the plan's step 9 reads as "fix the obvious a11y code smells" rather than "prove it works on his phone."

**Recommended change:** Add a dedicated mobile/responsive AC set to step 9 (or a new step 9b): minimum touch target size, verified layout at a phone-width viewport, a stated contrast target, and explicit loading/error recovery behavior — not just the accessibility-attribute fixes currently listed.

## 7. Tests that prove mechanism, not user-visible correctness

- Step 1's "0 of 743 bookings fail to join" is an internal diagnostic, not a correctness proof on its own — fine as a supplementary check, but the plan should be explicit that the *booking-ID regression tests* (checked via the actual HTTP response) are the real correctness evidence, and the join-count is secondary.
- Step 4's AC ("assert each role's expected detail-vs-redacted conflict shape") tests the JSON shape, not the end-to-end guarantee a skeptical reviewer actually cares about: *can a foreman, through any combination of fields in the response, determine another site's operator's identity?* That's a stronger, adversarially-framed test than "does this key exist." **Recommend adding at least one test phrased that way**, not just a shape assertion.
- Step 9's "automated label/role assertions in component tests" proves attributes exist, not that a keyboard-only user can actually complete "check availability" end to end, or that a screen reader announces something coherent. **Recommend an explicit, required manual (or axe/Playwright-driven) keyboard walkthrough as its own checklist item**, distinct from and in addition to the unit-level attribute tests — attribute presence and usable experience are not the same proof.

## 8. Scope/sequencing risk against the 4-hour cap

- **Step 1 is the plan's single biggest schedule risk, and it violates the plan-first skill's own rule.** It bundles four distinct, individually fiddly fixes (overlap semantics, 4-format date parsing, status filtering, tag normalization) into one step with one checkpoint. `plan-first` explicitly asks for "small, ordered steps, each independently testable and committable" — step 1 isn't that. If the date-format parser (the hardest piece) runs long or breaks something, there's no partial-credit checkpoint inside it, and everything downstream (steps 4, 7, 11) is blocked behind it. **Recommend splitting step 1 into 1a (cancelled-exclusion, trivial) → 1b (overlap semantics, trivial) → 1c (date normalization, the real work) → 1d (tag normalization)**, each committed separately.
- **No relative effort sizing anywhere.** I correctly avoided *guessing elapsed time* (per your earlier instruction), but I also omitted *relative effort estimates per step* entirely, which isn't the same restriction — the plan gives you no way to self-check pace against the clock you're tracking. **Recommend adding rough S/M/L or minute-range tags per step.**
- **Security review is scheduled last, with no buffer.** Step 10 is the only place security gets explicitly re-checked, after all nine other steps — but steps 2–3 (auth, PII) are exactly where this review just found two new High-severity gaps (alg-pinning, daily-rate leak). If time runs out before step 10, the security-critical work goes unreviewed by design. **Recommend an interim security checkpoint immediately after step 3** (auth + PII + authz core), not only a single pass at the end.
- **Step 4's dependency on A5 sign-off isn't flagged as reorderable.** Steps 2, 3, 5, 6 have no dependency on A5 at all and could proceed while sign-off is pending, but the plan's ordering reads as strictly sequential. **Recommend explicitly marking which steps are independent of the open A5 decision.**

## 9. Database/transaction assumptions — in anticipation of Part 2

The Part 1 plan is silent here by design (read-only, correctly out of scope), but you asked me to inspect what it leaves unaddressed. Explaining the mechanism, not designing one:

**How an unsafe check-then-insert lets two simultaneous reservations both succeed:** A naive handler does (1) `SELECT` for conflicting bookings on the target asset/window, (2) if none found, `INSERT` the new booking, (3) return success. With Go's `database/sql` connection pool, two concurrent requests for the *same* asset and *overlapping* times can each get their own pooled connection and run step 1 concurrently — both see zero conflicts, because neither has inserted yet. Both then proceed to step 2 and both `INSERT` succeed, because there is no `UNIQUE`/exclusion constraint (confirmed: zero constraints anywhere in `db/schema.sql`) and no lock tying the SELECT to the INSERT against *other* transactions. This is the exact same shape as the 18 confirmed-vs-confirmed double-bookings already found sitting in the seed data (row 14 above) — Part 2, built naively, reproduces that failure mode programmatically instead of by spreadsheet accident. Even wrapping check+insert in `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` (which this session's own concurrency experiment proved *does* correctly serialize writers) only closes the hole if **every** write path uses it consistently and the resulting lock error is caught and turned into a clear "someone else just booked this" response — not a generic crash, which would satisfy "must not both succeed" while badly failing Marcus's "tell the second guy right away."

**Questions Part 2 must resolve (not answered here):**
1. Isolation mechanism: `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` per request, an application-level serialization point, or a SQLite-compatible substitute for a true exclusion constraint (SQLite has none natively)?
2. How, and how fast, does the losing request get told — synchronous `409`, or something else — to satisfy "tell the second guy right away"?
3. Does a tentative hold block a later confirm attempt in the *write* path, re-raising A1 in a concurrency context, not just a read-availability one?
4. Retry policy on lock contention under ordinary (non-adversarial) load: zero retries, or bounded retry-with-backoff inside one request?
5. Does the guarantee need to hold across multiple API instances (the README asks this explicitly for Part 3A) — is Part 2 single-instance-only by design, with multi-instance explicitly deferred, or does it need to be designed for that from the start?
6. Does Part 2's own acceptance criteria need the "fire many simultaneous requests, exactly one wins" proof test itself, or is that proof test Part 3A's job while Part 2 only builds the mechanism? The README's Part 2 bullet ("must not both succeed, even at the same instant") and Part 3A bullet ("write a test that fires many simultaneous reservation requests") read as overlapping asks — Part 2's plan needs to explicitly draw this line.
7. Is operator double-booking (same operator, overlapping times, different equipment) in scope for the same mechanism, or a separate problem? The README's Part 2 bullet is equipment-focused; nothing currently guards the operator side.

These are listed as open questions for Part 2's own plan and ADR, per your instruction — I haven't chosen among them.

---

## Summary: recommended plan revisions before implementation begins

1. Split step 1 into 1a–1d with independent checkpoints.
2. Add the equipment-field sensitivity gap (`daily_rate_usd`, `notes`) to A5/A6 and to step 3's scope.
3. Close the `maintenance.status`-vs-`available` seam with an explicit combining rule and AC (§5's main finding) — this is the one I'd block implementation on.
4. Add cold-start/pre-first-fetch state handling to step 7's AC.
5. Add the missing JWT `alg`-pinning AC to step 2.
6. Narrow `safety_manager`'s default access in A5; split subcontractor visibility out of A5 as its own, more site-scoped default.
7. Add a dedicated mobile/responsive/contrast AC set (step 9b).
8. Add effort sizing per step; mark steps 2/3/5/6 as reorderable ahead of A5 sign-off; move a security checkpoint to right after step 3.
9. Add the mechanical DST and site-local-time cross-check before relying on A3.

No files changed in this review. Waiting for your call on which of these to fold into the plan before implementation starts.

Fold in — blocking, don’t start coding without these:

69	
70	This isn't really a multi-option design decision — it's a bug fix with one obviously correct answer — so no Options section here; stated plainly instead:
71	
72	- **Overlap test**: `booking.start < query.end AND booking.end > query.start` (strict inequalities — a booking that ends exactly when the query starts, or vice versa, does **not** conflict; this matches what scenarios 10/11 showed happening today, just for the wrong reason).
73	- **Status filter**: exclude `status='cancelled'` unconditionally (A2). Include `confirmed` and `tentative` per A1's default, tagging which in the response.
74	- **Normalization**: on read, parse all 4 observed formats into a single comparable instant, applying `sites.timezone` to naive values per A3, before running the overlap test. Do this once, in one function, covered by unit tests against the specific booking IDs in the evidence table (not just happy-path dates).
75	- **Asset-tag join**: normalize both sides (`equipment.asset_tag`, `bookings.asset_tag`) via A4's rule before joining; log (don't silently drop) anything that still fails to match.
76	
77	## FleetCare degraded-mode decision
78	
79	**Options considered:**
80	
81	1. **Call FleetCare synchronously per availability request.** Simplest to write; directly violates "behave sensibly when FleetCare is slow/down/rate-limited" — a single slow request (measured up to 5s, or a 30s hang) becomes Marcus's page load.
82	2. **TTL cache, lazily refreshed via the `/v1/maintenance/batch` endpoint (max 25 tags/call → 3 calls for 60 assets), bounded per-call timeout, no synchronous retry, serve last-known-good on failure, mark data explicitly stale past a threshold.**
83	3. **Background poller/circuit-breaker**, refreshing independently of the request path with exponential backoff on repeated failures. Most robust, more code than 4 hours affords alongside everything else in scope.
84	
85	**Chosen: Option 2**, with concrete defaults (tune later, these are two config constants, not an architecture):
86	- Cache TTL: 5 minutes (maintenance windows are planned days ahead; this is nowhere near FleetCare's 20req/10s limit — 3 calls per refresh).
87	- Per-call client timeout: 3s (comfortably above the mock's measured 2.5–5s "slow" case most of the time, well below the 30s hang case — bounded, as required).
88	- No synchronous retry on failure (fail fast, serve cache).
89	- **Representing unknown/stale availability**: do **not** collapse "FleetCare unreachable" into either `available:true` or `available:false` on the booking-derived field. Add a separate `maintenance: {status: "ok"|"in_maintenance"|"unknown", as_of: <timestamp>}` object. `in_maintenance` forces the item to read as unavailable regardless of bookings. `unknown` (cache empty or older than TTL×3 with a failed refresh attempt) is surfaced explicitly rather than defaulting to "ok" — this is the one place Dana's #1 complaint can recur if we get it wrong, so unknown must never silently read as fine.
90	
91	## Role/site visibility — authorization boundaries to enforce
92	
93	Per A5 (pending sign-off): the handler must read `UserFrom(r)` and apply, in order:
94	1. Reject if no valid, signature-verified token (fixes row 7).
95	2. Compute availability fleet-wide (booking + FleetCare logic unchanged by role).
96	3. For each item with a conflict, include full `conflict` detail only if `user.role in {ops_director, safety_manager}` **or** (`user.role in {superintendent, foreman}` **and** `conflict.site_id in user.site_ids`). Otherwise, return `conflict: {exists: true}` with no site/operator/time detail.
97	4. Never include any operator field in any response (A6) — not even for roles that can see full conflict detail; that's a different endpoint if it's ever needed.

101	Each step independently committable; checkpoint after each per the `checkpoint` skill.
102	
103	| Step | Work | Required? | Acceptance criteria (test-first per `write-tests`) |
104	|---|---|---|---|
105	| 1 | Conflict-detection rewrite: overlap semantics, status filter, date normalization, asset-tag normalization (one coherent function, since they're entangled) | **Required** | Regression tests on the exact evidenced booking IDs (`BK-1005`,`BK-1360`,`BK-1572`,`BK-1368`,`BK-1117`) plus the boundary/adjacent/partial-overlap geometries already proven live. Data-quality test: 0 of 743 bookings fail to join post-normalization (mechanical count, asserted in test). |
106	| 2 | JWT verification (real signature check, `exp` check); clean `401` on missing/empty/malformed/invalid-signature tokens, never 500, never silent pass-through | **Required** | Tests for all 4 malformed-token shapes already reproduced live, plus a validly-signed-but-expired token, plus a validly-signed token with a tampered payload |
107	| 3 | Strip operator PII from availability response entirely (A6) | **Required** | Response schema test: no PII field names present anywhere in the payload, for any role |
108	| 4 | Role/site authorization on conflict detail (A5 default) | **Required, pending A5 sign-off** | 4-role test matrix (already proven live as *failing* today) — assert each role's expected detail-vs-redacted conflict shape |
109	| 5 | Hygiene: explicit CORS allow-list, stop logging full headers, generic error body on 500 (no stack trace to client; still log server-side without `Authorization`) | **Required** | Test that a 500 response body contains no stack trace or file path; test that a request log line doesn't contain the literal string "Authorization" |
110	| 6 | Query validation: `start`/`end` required and parseable → 400 with a clear message otherwise; parameterize the `type` filter (fixes SQLi) | **Required** | Missing-params test → 400 (not 200-everything-available); SQLi payload test → 0 unexpected rows, not all 60 |
111	| 7 | FleetCare client + TTL cache + `maintenance` field (see degraded-mode decision) | **Required** | Unit tests against the mock with `CHAOS_SEED` values already computed this session (503, slow, truncated, hang) proving: bounded total latency, cache served on failure, `maintenance.status` correctly reflects `in_maintenance`/`ok`/`unknown`. Integration test: `MC-004` on 2026-10-02 now returns unavailable due to maintenance, matching FleetCare's mock data. |
112	| 8 | Frontend: loading state, empty state (zero results for a filter), error state (fetch failure/4xx/5xx), distinguishable from each other | **Required** | Manual + component test per state; no state silently falls through to a blank or stale list |
113	| 9 | Frontend accessibility: restore focus outline, label all form controls, real `<button>`/keyboard-operable controls for "Log out" and cards, remove `user-scalable=no`, add a text/icon signal alongside the color dot | **Required** | Keyboard-only walkthrough (tab to every control, operate with Enter/Space); automated label/role assertions in component tests |
114	| 10 | `security-review` skill pass over the full diff before calling Part 1 done | **Required** | Findings written to `docs/reviews/`, top 3 summarized, nothing silently fixed outside this plan's scope |
115	| 11 | *(stretch, time-boxed)* Half-day inter-site travel buffer, flat 12h, all equipment types (A7 default) | Optional — attempt last, only if time remains | Test: an asset booked at Site A ending <12h before a Site B booking starts reads unavailable in the gap |

Steps 8–9 depend on steps 1–7 only for integration testing, not for their own logic — frontend accessibility work can proceed in parallel if time allows.

124	- **Stopping point within the time budget**: you're tracking elapsed time yourself, so I'm not estimating a clock position. ## Correct overlap semantics, statuses, and date normalization (the core fix)

This isn't really a multi-option design decision — it's a bug fix with one obviously correct answer — so no Options section here; stated plainly instead:

- **Overlap test**: `booking.start < query.end AND booking.end > query.start` (strict inequalities — a booking that ends exactly when the query starts, or vice versa, does **not** conflict; this matches what scenarios 10/11 showed happening today, just for the wrong reason).
- **Status filter**: exclude `status='cancelled'` unconditionally (A2). Include `confirmed` and `tentative` per A1's default, tagging which in the response.
- **Normalization**: on read, parse all 4 observed formats into a single comparable instant, applying `sites.timezone` to naive values per A3, before running the overlap test. Do this once, in one function, covered by unit tests against the specific booking IDs in the evidence table (not just happy-path dates).
- **Asset-tag join**: normalize both sides (`equipment.asset_tag`, `bookings.asset_tag`) via A4's rule before joining; log (don't silently drop) anything that still fails to match.

## FleetCare degraded-mode decision

**Options considered:**

1. **Call FleetCare synchronously per availability request.** Simplest to write; directly violates "behave sensibly when FleetCare is slow/down/rate-limited" — a single slow request (measured up to 5s, or a 30s hang) becomes Marcus's page load.
2. **TTL cache, lazily refreshed via the `/v1/maintenance/batch` endpoint (max 25 tags/call → 3 calls for 60 assets), bounded per-call timeout, no synchronous retry, serve last-known-good on failure, mark data explicitly stale past a threshold.**
3. **Background poller/circuit-breaker**, refreshing independently of the request path with exponential backoff on repeated failures. Most robust, more code than 4 hours affords alongside everything else in scope.

**Chosen: Option 2**, with concrete defaults (tune later, these are two config constants, not an architecture):
- Cache TTL: 5 minutes (maintenance windows are planned days ahead; this is nowhere near FleetCare's 20req/10s limit — 3 calls per refresh).
- Per-call client timeout: 3s (comfortably above the mock's measured 2.5–5s "slow" case most of the time, well below the 30s hang case — bounded, as required).
- No synchronous retry on failure (fail fast, serve cache).
- **Representing unknown/stale availability**: do **not** collapse "FleetCare unreachable" into either `available:true` or `available:false` on the booking-derived field. Add a separate `maintenance: {status: "ok"|"in_maintenance"|"unknown", as_of: <timestamp>}` object. `in_maintenance` forces the item to read as unavailable regardless of bookings. `unknown` (cache empty or older than TTL×3 with a failed refresh attempt) is surfaced explicitly rather than defaulting to "ok" — this is the one place Dana's #1 complaint can recur if we get it wrong, so unknown must never silently read as fine.

## Role/site visibility — authorization boundaries to enforce

Per A5 (pending sign-off): the handler must read `UserFrom(r)` and apply, in order:
1. Reject if no valid, signature-verified token (fixes row 7).
2. Compute availability fleet-wide (booking + FleetCare logic unchanged by role).
3. For each item with a conflict, include full `conflict` detail only if `user.role in {ops_director, safety_manager}` **or** (`user.role in {superintendent, foreman}` **and** `conflict.site_id in user.site_ids`). Otherwise, return `conflict: {exists: true}` with no site/operator/time detail.
4. Never include any operator field in any response (A6) — not even for roles that can see full conflict detail; that's a different endpoint if it's ever needed.

**Revised after review (this is now a blocking spec, not an open seam):** the first version of this plan added a separate `maintenance.status` field and left it to *some future consumer* to combine it with `available`. A skeptical review correctly flagged that as the same failure mode this whole plan exists to fix, just moved one layer down — if nothing is ever wired up to read `maintenance.status`, equipment with unknown or in-maintenance FleetCare data renders as a plain green `available:true`, which is Dana's complaint, reproduced by the fix itself. Closing it at the data model, not by convention:

- **`available` is computed as `bookingAvailable AND maintenance.status == "ok"`.** `maintenance.status` is not a side channel a consumer can forget to check — it's baked into the one boolean the frontend already renders. `in_maintenance` and `unknown` both force `available:false`.
- `maintenance: {status: "ok"|"in_maintenance"|"unknown", as_of: <timestamp>}` is still returned alongside, for detail/debugging (e.g. so the UI can distinguish "actually booked" from "maintenance data unknown" in its copy), but it is no longer the only thing standing between a user and a false "available."
- **Cold start is explicitly "unknown," never "ok."** Before the cache has ever been successfully populated (server just started, or restarted mid-demo), there is no last-known-good to fall back to. The initial/zero-value state of the cache **must** be `"unknown"`, not an empty-but-valid-looking maintenance list — an uninitialized cache that defaults to "no windows found" is indistinguishable from "confirmed clean" and fails open exactly like the inherited bug. This is a required, explicitly tested state, not an edge case left to whatever the zero-value happens to be.
- This is intentionally conservative: equipment shows unavailable while maintenance data is merely unknown, even though it's probably fine. That's the correct bias given what this plan is for — Dana's complaint is about false *positives* on "available," not false negatives on "unavailable."

Do this once, in one function, covered by unit tests against the specific booking IDs in the evidence table (not just happy-path dates).
75	- **Asset-tag join**: normalize both sides (`equipment.asset_tag`, `bookings.asset_tag`) via A4's rule before joining; log (don't silently drop) anything that still fails to match.
76	- **One overlap function, used twice.** The inherited bug (row 1) exists because the containment check was written once, wrong, in one place. Step 7's FleetCare maintenance-window check **must call the same overlap-test function** defined here for bookings — not a second, separately-written comparison. Writing an independent overlap check for maintenance windows is how this exact bug reappears under a different name. This is a hard requirement on step 7, not a style preference.

79

81	
82	1. **Call FleetCare synchronously per availability request.** Simplest to write; directly violates "behave sensibly when FleetCare is slow/down/rate-limited" — a single slow request (measured up to 5s, or a 30s hang) becomes Marcus's page load.
83	2. **TTL cache, lazily refreshed via the `/v1/maintenance/batch` endpoint (max 25 tags/call → 3 calls for 60 assets), bounded per-call timeout, no synchronous retry, serve last-known-good on failure, mark data explicitly stale past a threshold.**
84	3. **Background poller/circuit-breaker**, refreshing independently of the request path with exponential backoff on repeated failures. Most robust, more code than 4 hours affords alongside everything else in scope.
85	
86	**Chosen: Option 2**, with concrete defaults (tune later, these are two config constants, not an architecture):
87	- Cache TTL: 5 minutes (maintenance windows are planned days ahead; this is nowhere near FleetCare's 20req/10s limit — 3 calls per refresh).
88	- Per-call client timeout: 3s (comfortably above the mock's measured 2.5–5s "slow" case most of the time, well below the 30s hang case — bounded, as required).
89	- No synchronous retry on failure (fail fast, serve cache).
90

95	- **Cold start is explicitly "unknown," never "ok."** Before the cache has ever been successfully populated (server just started, or restarted mid-demo), there is no last-known-good to fall back to. - **Status filter**: exclude `status='cancelled'` unconditionally (A2). Include `confirmed` and `tentative` per A1's default, tagging which in the response.
- **Normalization**: on read, parse all 4 observed formats into a single comparable instant, applying `sites.timezone` to naive values per A3, before running the overlap test. Do this once, in one function, covered by unit tests against the specific booking IDs in the evidence table (not just happy-path dates).
- **Asset-tag join**: normalize both sides (`equipment.asset_tag`, `bookings.asset_tag`) via A4's rule before joining; log (don't silently drop) anything that still fails to match.
- **One overlap function, used twice.** The inherited bug (row 1) exists because the containment check was written once, wrong, in one place. Step 7's FleetCare maintenance-window check **must call the same overlap-test function** defined here for bookings — not a second, separately-written comparison. Writing an independent overlap check for maintenance windows is how this exact bug reappears under a different name. This is a hard requirement on step 7, not a style preference.

## FleetCare degraded-mode decision

**Options considered:**

1. **Call FleetCare synchronously per availability request.** Simplest to write; directly violates "behave sensibly when FleetCare is slow/down/rate-limited" — a single slow request (measured up to 5s, or a 30s hang) becomes Marcus's page load.
2. **TTL cache, lazily refreshed via the `/v1/maintenance/batch` endpoint (max 25 tags/call → 3 calls for 60 assets), bounded per-call timeout, no synchronous retry, serve last-known-good on failure, mark data explicitly stale past a threshold.**
3. **Background poller/circuit-breaker**, refreshing independently of the request path with exponential backoff on repeated failures. Most robust, more code than 4 hours affords alongside everything else in scope.

**Chosen: Option 2**, with concrete defaults (tune later, these are two config constants, not an architecture):
- Cache TTL: 5 minutes (maintenance windows are planned days ahead; this is nowhere near FleetCare's 20req/10s limit — 3 calls per refresh).
- Per-call client timeout: 3s (comfortably above the mock's measured 2.5–5s "slow" case most of the time, well below the 30s hang case — bounded, as required).
- No synchronous retry on failure (fail fast, serve cache).

**Revised after review (this is now a blocking spec, not an open seam):** the first version of this plan added a separate `maintenance.status` field and left it to *some future consumer* to combine it with `available`. A skeptical review correctly flagged that as the same failure mode this whole plan exists to fix, just moved one layer down — if nothing is ever wired up to read `maintenance.status`, equipment with unknown or in-maintenance FleetCare data renders as a plain green `available:true`, which is Dana's complaint, reproduced by the fix itself. - **`available` is computed as `bookingAvailable AND maintenance.status == "ok"`.** `maintenance.status` is not a side channel a consumer can forget to check — it's baked into the one boolean the frontend already renders. `in_maintenance` and `unknown` both force `available:false`.

- **Cold start is explicitly "unknown," never "ok."** Before the cache has ever been successfully populated (server just started, or restarted mid-demo), there is no last-known-good to fall back to. The initial/zero-value state of the cache **must** be `"unknown"`, not an empty-but-valid-looking maintenance list — an uninitialized cache that defaults to "no windows found" is indistinguishable from "confirmed clean" and fails open exactly like the inherited bug. This is a required, explicitly tested state, not an edge case left to whatever the zero-value happens to be.

The reviewed Part 0/1 plan is approved. Implement only its in-scope work. Work through all six increments below, IN ORDER, to actual completion (green tests, checkpointed, committed) before any Part 2 planning or implementation begins. Do not let Part 2 feel more urgent or interesting than finishing this list -- if we get partway through Part 1 and start discussing Part 2, stop and point that out to me rather than going along with it.

Use the write-tests skill before each behavior change. First enumerate the scenarios in a table; then write focused tests, demonstrate the relevant tests fail when practical, implement the behavior, and rerun the tests.

1. Correct booking-overlap and date-window behavior.
2. Integrate FleetCare maintenance windows and the approved degraded-mode policy.
3. Enforce role/site filtering and remove unnecessary sensitive fields from responses.
4. Correct API validation and actionable error behavior.
5. Implement the frontend loading, empty, error, and retry states.
6. Improve one-handed mobile use, contrast, keyboard interaction, visible focus, and accessible status messages.

FleetCare specifics:
- Treat the vendor API as immutable.
- Respect its documented batch maximum of 25 assets and rate limit of 20 requests per 10 seconds.
- Use batching where appropriate rather than blindly making one vendor request per asset.
- Bound request timeouts and retries. Respect rate-limit responses and avoid retry storms.
- If caching is approved, document its freshness and outage behavior.
- Never silently treat an unavailable, invalid, timed-out, or unknown FleetCare result as confirmed available. Distinguish confirmed availability from unknown status in the API/UI contract.

Test overlap boundaries, existing booking statuses, maintenance-window intersections, invalid windows, vendor timeouts, 429/5xx errors, malformed data, and authorization across sites. Tests must be deterministic and must not depend on the vendor mock's random chaos.

If you introduce a new validation rule or database-level invariant (e.g. a stricter date parse, a uniqueness check, a trigger), run it against a full reseed of the REAL historical data, not just synthetic fixtures, before assuming it's safe. If the real data already violates the new rule, that is itself a finding worth reporting -- surface it explicitly, don't silently weaken the rule or hide the data to make the seed pass.

Before relying on a specific driver, pragma, or library behavior you haven't personally verified (a SQLite locking mode, a connection pool setting, anything whose exact semantics you're inferring from documentation rather than having tested), write a small throwaway script that empirically proves it does what you think, before building the real implementation on top of it.

Do not modify data/ or services/maintenance-api/. Do not silently expand scope when you discover new defects; document them and tell me.

After each independently completed behavior, run the relevant tests, update the approved plan and docs/plan/PROGRESS.md, invoke the checkpoint skill, and suggest a focused conventional commit.

At this checkpoint, report exactly what passed and what remains unverified. Do not call Part 1 complete if its security and functional acceptance criteria have not been verified, and do not call it complete if any of the six increments above is still outstanding.
